\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})}\,\text{d}x & =-2\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})|+C\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Calculate $\displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{\sin x}\left(\cot x + \sin^2 x\right)\,\textrm d x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We multiply out the parentheses and then use the identity $\dfrac{1}{\sin x } = \csc x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}(\operatorname{cot}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{cot}⁡x+\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot {sin}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\operatorname{csc}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{cot}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,\text{d}x+\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{csc}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Integrating a Quotient of Trigonometric Functions Using Trigonometric Identities
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We can write the integral as

$$
\int_0^{\pi/3} \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos^2 x}\,\textrm d x =  \int_0^{\pi/3} \dfrac{1}{\cos x}\cdot \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\,\textrm d x.
$$

We then use the fact that $\dfrac{\sin x }{\cos x}  = \tan x$ and $\dfrac{1}{\cos x} = \sec x$ to express this as

$$
\int_0^{\pi/3} \sec x\tan x\,\textrm d x,
$$

which is a standard trigonometric integral. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x{|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sec}⁡(0) \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Integrating a Trigonometric Expression Using Identities and Substitution
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We use the identity $\tan 2x = \dfrac{\sin 2x}{\cos 2x}$ and rewrite the integral as

$$
\int \tan{2x}\,\textrm d x = \int \dfrac{\sin{2x}}{\cos 2x}\,\textrm d x.
$$

Notice that the numerator of the integrand is proportional to the derivative of the denominator. So, we can solve this by substitution.

Let $u=\cos 2x.$ Then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=-2 \sin 2x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad -\dfrac 1 2 \,\textrm d u= \sin 2x \, \textrm d x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡2x|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)^{-1}|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sec}⁡2x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we want to calculate the integral

$$
\displaystyle \int\dfrac{1}{\sin^2x}\,\textrm d x.
$$

At first glance, this looks kind of tricky. However, if we use the identity $\dfrac{1}{\sin x} = \csc x,$ we can rewrite the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=\int {(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x})}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\int {csc}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we see that this is just a standard trigonometric integral:

$$
\int\dfrac{1}{\sin^2x}\,\textrm d x  =  \int\csc^2 x\,\textrm d x =-\cot x + C
$$

When confronted with a tricky-looking trigonometric integral, we can often reduce it to a standard integral using a trigonometric identity.
